# C5. The cross-country test {#esc-oecd26}

Section {{< var p.sec_esc_crossSection >}} of the paper tests the model on the countries of figure
{{< var p.fig_US_OECDdata >}}. Every country keeps its own workers per retiree, corrected for its gap to the U.S.
statutory retirement age, its income distribution, its observed design and its propensities to vote by income group,
from the CSES; Luxembourg, which has no CSES survey and enforces compulsory voting, votes at the same rate in every
income group. Every country takes from the U.S. the discount factor $\beta$ and the cost of redistribution as the
elasticity $\varepsilon$, so that country $n$ faces $\lambda_{n,t} = \varepsilon\,\Pi_{n,t}/R_{n,t}$ at its own ratio
of the pay-as-you-go return to the market return. Layer 2 calibrates each country's political weight of the old
$\omega$ to its pension spending at its observed design; layer 1 gives every country the mean of these weights. The
U.S. anchor, where $\omega$ and $\varepsilon$ are calibrated, is measured as every other country is (appendix
{{< var p.app_oecd26_anchor >}} of the paper). This page shows the variants of appendix {{< var p.app_oecd26 >}} in
full, and the test with Luxembourg left out and with layer 1 at the U.S. political weight.

## The paper's specification {#esc-oecd26-paper}

The paper reports the test in figure {{< var p.fig_OECD26_layer1 >}} and table {{< var p.table_OECD26_slopes >}}, and
each country's political weight and design in layer 2 in table {{< var p.table_OECD26_omega >}}. Table
{{< var p.table_OECD26_variants >}} gives the slopes under each variant below, and figures
{{< var p.fig_OECD26_thetaFitPopulation >}} and {{< var p.fig_OECD26_thetaFitMeasure >}} the predicted designs.

## Other population data {#esc-oecd26-population}

Workers per retiree as the population data give them, and corrected for each country's gap to the U.S. effective age
of labour-market exit in place of the statutory age. The data side of the test does not depend on them. The second
layer hardly moves under either reading, since its political weights are calibrated to spending. In the first layer
the exit age leaves the test close to the paper's. With workers per retiree uncorrected, Luxembourg, whose population
grew fastest, chooses a design close to the Beveridgean corner, and the predicted designs track the observed ones much
less closely; without Luxembourg they track them about as closely as under either correction (appendix
{{< var p.app_oecd26_readings >}} of the paper).

## Other measures of the design {#esc-oecd26-measure}

Each measure of the design is its own cross-section: the data and the model are calibrated to it, on the countries
where it is defined, with the U.S. anchor recalibrated under it (appendix {{< var p.app_oecd26_readings >}} of the
paper). The public tier on 23 countries leaves the test as it is. Under all mandatory tiers the relations keep their
signs, while the first layer predicts the design less well, in part because it puts Iceland, which only this measure
covers, close to the Beveridgean corner.

## Luxembourg left out {#esc-oecd26-luxembourg}

The test on the countries with a CSES survey, all but Luxembourg. Without Luxembourg the data's index falls more steeply
with population growth than with it, and the index of the model's first layer falls much less steeply than the data's.

{{< include _generated/exhibits/OECD26_Layer1_cses.qmd >}}

{{< include _generated/exhibits/OECD26_Slopes_cses.qmd >}}

## Layer 1 at the U.S. political weight {#esc-oecd26-omegaUS}

Every country in layer 1 at the U.S. $\omega$ in place of the mean of layer 2's weights. Layer 2 is the paper's. At
the U.S. weight, above that mean, the countries choose somewhat more Bismarckian designs and spend more, while the
cross-section is nearly the paper's: the predicted designs track the observed ones about as closely, and every slope
keeps its sign.

{{< include _generated/exhibits/OECD26_Layer1_omegaUS.qmd >}}

{{< include _generated/exhibits/OECD26_Slopes_omegaUS.qmd >}}

## The countries outside the test {#esc-oecd26-all}

Figure {{< var p.fig_US_OECDdata >}}, and so the test, leaves out the OECD members before 2000 that the model does not
represent. In Korea, Mexico and Turkey a large share of employment is informal, and the model of sections
{{< var p.sec_oecd >}} and {{< var p.sec_esc >}} has no informal households. In Australia, Denmark, Iceland, the
Netherlands and Switzerland funded tiers pay a large share of mandatory benefits, or the public pension is tested
against them, where the model has a single public pay-as-you-go system. [D1](data.qmd) gives the data of the countries
the figure covers.
